title: Napster Launches
summary: Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker launch Napster, enabling peer-to-peer music sharing and disrupting the entire music industry.
narrative: Shawn Fanning is a 19-year-old dropout who builds a peer-to-peer file sharing network. Sean Parker sees the potential. They call it Napster after Fanning's nickname. You download the software, share your MP3 library, and search everyone else's. Within months, 20 million people are using it. The music industry panics. Metallica sues. Lars Ulrich goes to Congress. But you can't stop it. Napster changes the fundamental equation: music wants to be free. The industry will spend 20 years trying to catch up.
why_it_matters: Napster proved that digital distribution was what consumers wanted. It forced the music industry to eventually adopt streaming, and taught the lesson that piracy is a service problem.

title: DSL and Cable Modems Reach Mass Market
summary: DSL and cable internet services expand rapidly, beginning the slow death of dial-up and enabling always-on internet connections.
narrative: In 1999, most people connect to the internet through a 56k modem that ties up the phone line. But DSL and cable modems are arriving. Pacific Bell, EarthLink, and Comcast offer 'always-on' internet. It's faster. It doesn't block your phone. It costs more. But once you go broadband, you never go back. The always-on connection changes behavior. You don't 'go online' anymore. You're always online. This is the beginning of the always-connected world we live in now.
why_it_matters: Broadband enabled streaming media, online gaming, and the always-on internet. It was the infrastructure upgrade that made the modern internet possible.

title: Palm V PDA Released
summary: 3Com releases the Palm V, the sleekest personal digital assistant ever made, bringing handheld computing to the mainstream.
narrative: The Palm V is beautiful. Anodized aluminum. Thin. Syncs with your desktop via HotSync. Your contacts, calendar, and to-do list — always with you. Graffiti handwriting recognition lets you scribble notes on the screen. The price is $399. It's the first PDA that feels like a consumer product, not a business tool. Jeff Hawkins and Donna Dubinsky built Palm on the principle of simplicity. 10 million Palm devices will ship. The smartphone is coming. But in 1999, the Palm V is the coolest gadget in your pocket.
why_it_matters: The Palm V proved that handheld computing could be elegant and mainstream. It established the PDA market that the iPhone would eventually cannibalize.

title: EverQuest Launches
summary: Sony Online Entertainment launches EverQuest, the massively multiplayer online RPG that creates addiction, community, and a virtual economy.
narrative: Brad McQuaid and his team at Sony Online Entertainment build a 3D online world called Norrath. You create a character. You join a guild. You fight dragons. You lose your corpse and all your gear. You lose sleep. You lose relationships. EverQuest is so addictive it's called 'EverCrack.' At its peak, 550,000 players pay $12.95/month. It's not the first MMO — Ultima Online got there first. But EverQuest creates the template that World of Warcraft will perfect. Guilds, raids, loot, epics. The MMORPG genre is born.
why_it_matters: EverQuest created the MMORPG genre and proved that people would pay monthly for online gaming. It established the virtual economy and guild social structures that WoW would scale to millions.

title: 802.11b Wi-Fi Standard Released
summary: The IEEE ratifies 802.11b, the first widely-adopted Wi-Fi standard, enabling wireless networking at 11 Mbps.
narrative: The IEEE ratifies the 802.11b standard on September 16, 1999. It supports 11 Mbps — about 700 times faster than your 56k modem. You buy a $99 wireless access point. You plug it in. You can suddenly use the internet from your couch. No cables. The concept of 'Wi-Fi' enters the public vocabulary. Starbucks starts offering it in 2002. The coffee shop becomes the office. The airport becomes the living room. The tether is cut.
why_it_matters: 802.11b made wireless internet practical and affordable. It untethered computing from fixed locations, enabling the mobile revolution.

title: Y2K Panic Peaks
summary: The world prepares for the Year 2000 bug, with governments and businesses spending billions to prevent computer systems from crashing.
narrative: The Year 2000 bug — Y2K — is real. Computers stored years as two digits. When 99 becomes 00, will they think it's 1900? Will planes fall from the sky? Will nuclear reactors melt down? The US government creates the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion. Businesses spend $300 billion worldwide. People stockpile food and water. The media runs doomsday stories. When January 1, 2000 arrives, nothing happens. Was it a hoax? Or did the $300 billion fix work? Nobody knows for sure. But the world survived.
why_it_matters: Y2K was the first global technology panic. It showed how dependent civilization had become on computer systems, and how vulnerable those systems were to simple bugs.

title: The 'ILOVEYOU' Virus Preview
summary: Computer viruses become a mainstream concern as email worms spread rapidly and expose the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
narrative: The Melissa virus arrives in March 1999. It's an email worm that sends itself to the first 50 people in your Outlook address book. It crashes email servers. The FBI investigates. Then in 2000, ILOVEYOU will do even more damage. But in 1999, the lesson is clear: the internet connects everyone, and so it connects everyone's vulnerabilities. Your computer isn't just yours anymore. It's a node in a network. And networks can be weaponized.
why_it_matters: Email viruses exposed the security risks of internet-connected computing. They drove the antivirus industry and raised awareness about email security.

title: MP3.com Music Revolution
summary: MP3.com becomes the hub of independent music, enabling unsigned artists to reach audiences directly without record labels.
narrative: MP3.com lets anyone upload their music and share it with the world. No record label needed. No A&R guy to convince. Just upload and share. Thousands of independent artists flood the platform. It becomes the first true music social network. The major labels sue MP3.com for $17 billion. The site settles for $53 million and gets acquired by Vivendi Universal. But the lesson is learned: artists don't need labels anymore. The internet is the new record store.
why_it_matters: MP3.com proved that independent artists could reach audiences directly. It started the democratization of music distribution that Bandcamp, SoundCloud, and Spotify would continue.

title: Windows 2000 Released
summary: Microsoft releases Windows 2000, combining the stability of NT with consumer features and laying groundwork for Windows XP.
narrative: Windows 2000 is the operating system Microsoft needed. It takes the stability of Windows NT and adds plug-and-play, USB support, and better gaming. It's not for consumers — that's Windows 98's job. But businesses adopt it fast. It doesn't crash like Windows 95/98. It handles memory better. It's built on the NT kernel that will power Windows XP, Vista, 7, 10, and 11. Windows 2000 is the foundation Microsoft builds the next 20 years on.
why_it_matters: Windows 2000 unified Microsoft's consumer and enterprise lines. Its NT kernel became the basis for all modern Windows versions.

title: The Matrix Hits Theaters & Defines Cyberpunk Cool
summary: The Wachowskis' sci-fi masterpiece fused cyberpunk philosophy, anime stunts, and 'bullet time' visual effects.
narrative: Audiences were asked to take the red pill and woke up inside a simulated world. Keanu Reeves dodging bullets on a rooftop in slow-motion green phosphor tint became the visual wallpaper of the millennium. Everything from black leather trench coats, tiny sunglasses, and Nokia slider phones to philosophical debates about simulated reality seeped directly into global tech culture.
why_it_matters: The Matrix permanently encoded cyberpunk aesthetics and simulation anxiety into modern internet culture and cinema visual effects.

title: The Y2K Bug Panic & The Midnight Countdown
summary: Fears that older two-digit year computer systems would crash at midnight caused worldwide preparations and dread.
narrative: Doomsday preppers stockpiled canned peaches, bottled water, and generators, while airlines grounded midnight flights. Corporations and governments invested over $300 billion in heroic remediation efforts to rewrite legacy COBOL and database systems. When the clock struck midnight in Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York, the lights stayed on and computers hummed along peacefully, turning terror into celebration.
why_it_matters: The Y2K bug represented the first time global society collectively recognized its absolute dependency on silent digital infrastructure.

title: Britney Spears & Backstreet Boys Lead Teen Pop Mania
summary: Britney Spears' '...Baby One More Time' and the Backstreet Boys' 'Millennium' shattered music industry sales records.
narrative: MTV's studio in Times Square for Total Request Live (TRL) with Carson Daly became the screaming epicenter of American adolescence. Backstreet Boys' 'Millennium' sold over 1.1 million copies in its first week alone, while 17-year-old Britney Spears became an overnight pop titan. CD sales peaked at their all-time historical high just as Napster was quietly being born in a college dorm.
why_it_matters: It marked the commercial apex of the physical CD music industry right before digital file-sharing decentralized music distribution forever.
